item.title: Trajectories Through Parsons Problems: Making Student Difficulty Patterns Visible to Instructors
item.description: arXiv:2611.26799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing Parsons problem tools primarily focus on correctness, indicating whether a student solved a problem, but providing limited visibility into the underlying problem-solving process. Without that visibility, instructors cannot see which blocks caused repeated confusion or which distractors were consistently selected. We introduce Pulla, a Parsons problem tool that instruments programming assignments to capture fine-grained interaction data. We examine what these behavioral traces make visible to instructors, namely how long students take on a problem and how many moves they make, which recurring errors the distractors expose and how the class arrives at them, whether those errors follow a student from one problem to the next, and which students complete the whole assignment without a single error.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Prol, Juho Leinonen, Arto Hellas, Saleh Alkhamees, Amin Alipour

item.title: Explain Your Code: AI-Based Examination at Class Scale
item.description: arXiv:2611.26836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI has weakened the link between working code and a student's understanding of it. Oral examination, the traditional test of that understanding, does not scale to large courses. We report the full-course deployment of a three-agent AI system that examines students on their own code. The first, the examiner, asks three questions anchored to specific lines of the submission, adapting difficulty to each answer, in a 16-minute text dialogue. The other two grade: a code reviewer that never sees the examination and a grader without direct access to the code. Authorship is assessed separately and is advisory. The system examined 247 students in an operating systems course (three exercises, 546 sittings, two examination languages). The grader's oral score was uncorrelated with the same submission's code quality score (Spearman rho = -0.073, 95% CI [-0.205, 0.063], n = 216) yet tracked degree grade point average (rho = 0.419, [0.294, 0.523], n = 214), while automated test scores sat at the ceiling. The mean of a student's two oral scores correlated with grade point average at 0.468 ([0.353, 0.568], n = 210), within the range of grades in three single-semester courses built on programming assignments. Model spend averaged at most $1.37 per sitting. In surveys, students began skeptical of the AI examination and rated it more favorably after sitting it twice. These results indicate that examining students on their own code is feasible at class scale, and that its score relates to academic standing where the code quality score does not.
item.dc:creator: David Sarne (Department of Computer Science, Bar-Ilan University, Ramat Gan, Israel), Shachar Sagi (Department of Computer Science, Bar-Ilan University, Ramat Gan, Israel), Yossi Ben-Zion (Department of Physics, Bar-Ilan University, Ramat Gan, Israel)

item.title: AROMA: Understanding AI Support For Mental Well-being through Role Theory
item.description: arXiv:2611.26843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI supporters for mental well-being are becoming more prevalent. When these AI supporters start acting in ways beyond their expected function it leads to relational harm. Standard approaches to evaluating such AI supporters are limited to inspecting their efficacy in narrow task-specific settings, which do not explain these discrepancies in expected and actual behavior. To address this gap, we propose the AROMA (A Role-Oriented Model of Analysis) framework to provide a common role taxonomy for different support contexts. We developed AROMA using a theory-informed annotation of over 7,515 conversations from 13 datasets and propose eight "Role States" based on observed-not prescribed-behavior. We show these Role States vary according to the context of support; depict unique structural and temporal characteristics of AI supporters vis-a-vis Humans; and inform novel AI support prompting strategy for better role alignment. This framework provides a new lens to understand AI support failures.
item.dc:creator: Issac Ting, Ethan Pan, Koustuv Saha, Hua Shen, Kevin Chow, Vedant Das Swain

item.title: Comparing Visual Motion Patterns for Pedestrian Guidance with Multi-Display Signage: Two Field Studies
item.description: arXiv:2611.26984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public multi-display signage (MDS) has the potential to provide subtle pedestrian guidance through visual motion while retaining its conventional role in advertising and information delivery. However, it remains unclear how different visual motion patterns relate to pedestrian spatial distributions and how these relationships vary across deployment settings. We conducted two exploratory field studies in a museum, involving 18,402 pedestrian passages over 25 experimental days, to examine lateral positions in relation to stripe-motion contrast and coverage patterns. In Test Case 1 (TC1), involving predominantly one-way pedestrian flow, partial stripe presentation was associated with more leftward lateral positions than wider-coverage patterns in some comparisons, and lower contrast in full-screen stripes was not associated with a detectable reduction in the observed lateral bias. In Test Case 2 (TC2), conducted in a different spatial configuration permitting bidirectional walking, lateral positions differed by stripe-motion direction during one-way flow, but coverage effects on lateral position and stripe-advertisement differences in lateral position or passing-side choice were not significant. In both test cases, partial stripes received lower self-reported sickness ratings than full-screen stripes. These findings suggest that lower-contrast and reduced-motion-coverage designs hold practical potential for pedestrian guidance, with spatially restricted cues potentially allowing such guidance to coexist with existing advertising while reducing discomfort. At the same time, the contrasting patterns in TC1 and TC2 suggest that spatial context may shape how pedestrians respond to stripe coverage, highlighting the context-dependent suitability of visual-motion-based guidance and the need for further investigation.
item.dc:creator: Yuri Mikawa, Taiki Fukiage, Yuki Kubota, Takumi Yokosaka, Kazushi Maruya

item.title: Standard-Anchored Delegation in Teachers' Use of Generative AI
item.description: arXiv:2611.27533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Teachers who use generative AI must decide which parts of their work to hand over, while they remain accountable for what reaches students. We studied these decisions in Punjab, Pakistan, through a qualitatively driven mixed-methods study. We interviewed 13 teachers from government, private, NGO and vocational institutions, four administrators and one student, and coded each teacher's position on twelve educational tasks. Nine teachers accepted AI drafts or substantial assistance with lesson planning, but none accepted AI-drafted learning objectives, and eleven did not use AI to encourage or emotionally support students. Teachers who would accept AI marking required that the model be given a rubric or marking criteria. Building on assessment research and HCI work on verifiability, we call this pattern standard-anchored delegation: teachers handed a component of a task to AI when a standard outside the model, such as a textbook or rubric, defined a correct output and the teacher could apply that standard to the result. Having a standard was not always enough. Several government-school teachers did not use AI to mark quizzes even though the quizzes had answer keys, because they expected students to look for evidence of the teacher's effort. Checking AI output required subject knowledge and time, and private schools gave teachers more support for this than government schools did. Participants also read disclosure of AI use as a statement about whether the teacher had reviewed the work. We propose that teacher-facing AI tools ask for the relevant standard before generating and show each output beside it, and that schools account for the time that checking takes.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Saleh Farooq, Muhammad Ahmad Khan, Muhammad Jon Raza

item.title: GAZEAIDE: Recording Gaze Context for Research on AI-Assisted Development
item.description: arXiv:2611.27614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Developers increasingly review code they did not write, much of it generated by AI. Where they look while reading may indicate what is relevant to them, but tools rarely have access to this information. We demonstrate GAZEAIDE, an open-source research prototype for collecting it. Using a webcam, GAZEAIDE estimates which parts of the code a developer looks at and for how long, and records this viewing history together with the text shown on screen. Such context can serve different purposes: providing visual feedback on what has been viewed, guiding code review, and preparing context for a question, which a developer can choose to send to an AI assistant. An IntelliJ plugin records work in the editor; a browser companion records assistant conversations. Attendees can record a short session, replay their viewing history, and try these scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Heidi Albarazi, Ilya Zakharov, Ekaterina Koshchenko, Agnia Sergeyuk

item.title: Shared Understanding in Human-AI Teams: Coordination Continuity in Evolving Work
item.description: arXiv:2611.27746v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People are increasingly working with AI agents as part of extended, asynchronous workflows. In these settings, shared access to information does not guarantee a shared basis for action: goals, plans, and roles may persist while their current significance changes. We introduce coordination continuity, the extent to which collaborators sustain a workable basis for interdependent action as work progresses. Drawing on research on collaborative work, along with two qualitative team studies and a reflexive case from our own repository-based environment, we present a framework of three elements: durable representations of collaborative work; relative coordination properties that support interpretation of representations in the moment; and interaction mechanisms through which the status of representations can be understood and altered. We use a build-act-drift-rebuild heuristic and the notion of consequential moments to characterise when rebuilding may be needed. We draw eight design implications for collaborative AI infrastructure.
item.dc:creator: Si\^an Lindley, Britta Burlin, Christian Poelitz, Lev Tankelevitch, Richard Banks

item.title: Windchime: an Audiovisual Installation with Audio-Language Model implementations
item.description: arXiv:2611.26759v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Windchime is an audiovisual installation in which spoken language retrieves music and interactive animations from an artist authored corpus. A local Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) model transcribes each prompt while an audio-language model (ALM) embeds it and retrieval over 406 audio stems returns a soundscape with live coded Strudel fragments that layer into audio output. Simultaneously each spoken input results in retrieval of interactive Three.js animation scenes each containing unique tactile control via monome grid and arc hardware. Windchime distributes agency in three distinct directions; across the artist who authored the possible outputs, the ALM that influences what areas of the corpus can be retrieved, and the visitor whose spoken inputs result in multimodal embodied interaction.
item.dc:creator: Trent Eriksen, Celeste Betancur Gutierrez

item.title: Beyond Prompt Heuristics: Assessing Child Safety Alignment in LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2611.26965v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.
item.dc:creator: Anika Misra, Chimaobi Okite, Rada Mihalcea

item.title: Scalable Evaluation of Medical AI using Evidence-based Practice Recommendations
item.description: arXiv:2611.27007v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rigorously evaluating medical artificial intelligence (AI) requires testing open-ended clinical management across diverse presentations and stages of care. However, existing benchmarks rely on manual expert authoring, limiting coverage across conditions, conditional care pathways, and evolving guidelines. We develop an automated pipeline that extracts and verifies structured clinical criteria and branching decision trees from practice recommendations to generate scenarios spanning the care continuum, including nuanced presentations and practice variations across regions and guideline editions. Applied to 436 BMJ Best Practice clinical monographs (354 US, 82 International), this yields 3,200 scenarios spanning differential diagnosis, investigations, treatment, and complications, plus targeted suites for regional specificity (731 US/International pairs) and temporal freshness (630 scenarios). To grade responses, we develop a clinician-calibrated autorater that scores management plans on a 4-point rubric stratifying deviations by clinical severity. Across Gemini models, scaling improves adherence, while web search (+0.8 percentage points [pp] on average) and multi-sample synthesis (+2.2 pp) combine additively (+2.8 pp). In context, full monographs consistently trail condensed excerpts. On targeted suites, web search narrows international performance gaps (+4.2 pp) and improves adherence to newly updated guidance (+4.6 pp). In a study with Primary Care Physicians (n = 9) across 200 scenarios, AI assistance raises adherence from 50.5% to 70.0%, driven largely by fewer clinical omissions. Overall, our results demonstrate a scalable evaluation setup using an evidence-based corpus originally written to guide human clinical decision-making, and demonstrate its viability to assess medical AI and its assistance on clinician decision-making.
item.dc:creator: Teya Bergamaschi, Bijal Rajput, Akshay Goel, Matthew Thompson, Jacqueline Shreibati, Dave Steiner, Ashley Carrick, Mahvish Nagda, Dale R. Webster, Avinatan Hassidim, Katherine Chou, Yossi Matias, Po-Hsuan Cameron Chen, Christina Chen, Mike Schaekermann, Yun Liu, Anil Palepu

item.title: Omo: Giving Continuing AI-Agent Work a Place to Return To
item.description: arXiv:2611.27107v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI coding agents now keep working while the people who started them are away. Coming back is the hard part: a session list tells you which agent is where, but not what it was asked to do, what it changed, or what to tell it next. We present Omo, which gives each piece of continuing agent work a persistent place to return to. We built the idea twice. Omo Space is an open-source Minecraft mod in which rooms and screens that people build are live terminals on their own machine. Omo Theia brings the same rooms and desks into a customizable IDE, one step away from the editor and the Git patch. Both keep agent sessions running on the host after the view is closed. We describe the two systems, four lessons from building them, and a study designed to test whether returning to a place helps people pick up agent work correctly.
item.dc:creator: Kaviru Hapuarachchi, Harrison Edwards

item.title: On the Challenges of Using LLMs in High-Risk AI Recruitment: Guiding Questions for Legal Conformity with the AI Act
item.description: arXiv:2611.27462v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) imposes detailed obligations on providers of high-risk AI systems but offers limited operational guidance, particularly when these systems integrate third-party General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models. This paper introduces a toolkit that fosters the development of legal-by-design AI-assisted recruitment systems by translating the core legal obligations of the AI Act's conformity assessment---specifically Articles 9--15 and Annex IV---into techno-normative requirements and corresponding guiding questions. While recruitment pipelines may involve components with varying technical complexity and differing levels of algorithmic transparency, this paper focuses on the most challenging case: the integration of third-party GPAI models into critical stages of the selection process, including resume and job description parsing, applicant scoring, and shortlist generation. This scenario presents significant challenges for downstream providers of high-risk AI systems, as it underscores the difficulties in obtaining the technical information needed to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act's techno-normative requirements, both prior to and during market deployment. After introducing the toolkit and illustrating its application through a simplified example, the paper explores informational dependencies between upstream and downstream GPAI model providers. These dependencies may produce informational gaps across the AI supply chain, potentially hindering the collection of evidence necessary for the AI system provider to ensure legal compliance. The resulting lack of technical transparency negatively affects the deployer, who may struggle to maintain meaningful oversight of the system, and ultimately impacts the persons subject to the AI output.
item.dc:creator: Clara Punzi, Stefano Tramacere, Andrea Fedele, Sezer Kutluk, Roberto Pellungrini, Gizem Gezici, Paolo Baracco, Laura Castello, Eleonora Cusin, Eduardo Costa, Amedeo Giacovelli, Mario D'Almo, Fosca Giannotti, Dino Pedreschi, Marzio Di Vece

item.title: The Times They Are A-Changin': Tracking Global Trends through the Lens of Web Search
item.description: arXiv:2611.27613v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Human societies have always left traces of their collective priorities, from cave drawings and stone carvings to chronicles on papyrus and printed books. In the digital era, these traces increasingly emerge through social media footprints and web search behavior at a global scale. We construct the first large-scale longitudinal dataset of Google Year in Search trends, spanning 15 years, to characterize how collective public attention evolves across countries and time. Because search engines like Google and Bing do not publicly release raw search logs, Year in Search provides a rare cross-national archive of annually salient search interests. The dataset is supplemented with a manually curated, unified ten-category semantic taxonomy with strong inter-annotator agreement. We focus on four categories (Information Seeking, Personality, Entertainment, and Sports) to investigate how collective attention varies across geographic and socio-cultural contexts. Our analyses reveal a consistently glocalized structure of collective attention: countries converge strongly in profession-level personality attention while remaining differentiated in the specific individuals they search for, yet profession-level similarity is only weakly associated with geographic region and income group. Information seeking is globally dominated by politics and health, while regional distributions show varying degrees of divergence. Crisis periods are associated with both shared and regionally differentiated shifts. Entertainment and sports attention likewise combine globally prominent interests with regional differentiation. Overall, our findings suggest that web search data provide a valuable computational lens for observing collective attention at scale, acting as a living archive of how societal priorities vary across countries and change over time.
item.dc:creator: Anju Bhuiya, Hasim Ali, Kovvada Dhyana Vardhan, Abhijnan Chakraborty

item.title: Functional Flexibility in Generative AI Interfaces: Text Editing with LLMs through Conversations, Toolbars, and Prompts
item.description: arXiv:2410.10644v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many recent user interfaces (UIs) promise great flexibility via access to Large Language Models (LLMs) through prompting. This shifts efforts in accessing functionality from developers to users. However, is a maximum of functional flexibility always beneficial? We find: no -- and develop Functional Flexibility as a concept by reflecting on our long-term exploration of integrating LLMs into a text editor: In a prompt-elicitation survey, people (N=121) envisioned elaborate prompts for delegating flexible tasks to AI. In contrast, when interacting with a prototype (N=10), users preferred short command-like prompts, as prompting repeated functionality is tedious. Another prototype offered such commands in a toolbar, in addition to flexible prompting, leading users (N=12) to dynamically work with both. We contribute Functional Flexibility as a theoretical construct with analytical, critical, and constructive value. Overall, we encourage designing UIs for generative AI that go beyond free text prompting by explicitly considering functional flexibility in design.
item.dc:creator: Florian Lehmann, Daniel Buschek

item.title: "It Was a Magical Box": Understanding Practitioner Workflows and Needs in Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2509.16402v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optimization underpins decision-making in domains from healthcare to logistics, yet for many practitioners it remains a "magical box": powerful but opaque, difficult to use, and reliant on specialized expertise. While prior work has extensively studied machine learning workflows, the everyday practices of optimization model developers (OMDs) have received little attention. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 15 OMDs across diverse domains to examine how optimization is done in practice. Our findings reveal a highly iterative workflow spanning six stages: problem elicitation, data processing, model development, implementation, validation, and deployment. Importantly, we find that optimization practice is not only about algorithms that deliver better decisions, but is equally shaped by data and dialogue---the ongoing communication with stakeholders that enables problem framing, calibrated trust, and adoption. We discuss opportunities for future tooling that foregrounds data and dialogue alongside decision-making, opening new directions for human-centered optimization.
item.dc:creator: Connor Lawless, Jakob Schoeffer, Madeleine Udell

item.title: TopoPilot: Reliable Conversational Workflow Automation for Topological Data Analysis and Visualization
item.description: arXiv:2603.25063v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent agentic systems demonstrate that large language models can generate complex codebases from natural language prompts. Despite this progress, they present reliability concerns for scientific visualization due to invalid operations, subtle errors, and failure to resolve underspecified inputs. In this work, we introduce TopoPilot, a reliable and extensible agentic framework for automating complex scientific visualization workflows. We focus on topological data analysis and visualization as a primary use case, while designing the framework to generalize to broader visualization domains. TopoPilot employs a two-agent architecture: an orchestrator translates user prompts into workflows composed of atomic backend actions, while a verifier evaluates workflows prior to execution. Its modular design isolates components and supports new topological descriptors and domain-specific workflows without modifying the core system. It also employs numerous deterministic guardrails to ensure semantic consistency and accurate execution. To systematically improve reliability, we develop a taxonomy of failure modes and employ targeted safeguards for each class of error. Across 2,000 simulated multi-turn conversations spanning 100 prompts, including adversarial and infeasible requests, TopoPilot achieves a success rate exceeding 95%, compared with under 50% for a baseline without comprehensive guardrails and verification. We also show that TopoPilot outperforms Claude Code and Codex on similar prompts in terms of accuracy, completion time, and token usage.
item.dc:creator: Nathaniel Gorski, Shusen Liu, Bei Wang

item.title: TractorBeam: Personalized AI Sensemaking Support via Collaborative Machine Annotation
item.description: arXiv:2608.18994v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language model-based systems have become popular tools for sensemaking. Despite their capabilities, including expanding the scope of sensemaking to whole corpora, these systems still suffer from issues of factuality and provenance, while encouraging primarily top-down sensemaking. We present TractorBeam, a browser extension-based mixed-initiative system that uses collaborative annotation as an interface metaphor for sensemaking, re-framing language model (LM) outputs as suggested highlights in a process that we call collaborative machine annotation. This metaphor allows us to present LM results in-context on PDF documents, directly addressing concerns of provenance and factuality, while allowing users to iteratively construct mental schemata and queries for language models directly in the context of a document. Participants in our think-aloud and diary studies found that TractorBeam's collaborative annotation interface allowed them to iteratively construct useful, personalized highlighting systems, encouraged them to actively schematize their reading, and accomodated both top-down and bottom-up sensemaking.
item.dc:creator: Sireesh Gururaja, Nikolas Martelaro, Emma Strubell
